q: From which date did the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam and the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita come into force?
options: 1 January 2024, together with the DPDP Act's rules
1 July 2024, replacing the Evidence Act and the CrPC
28 April 2022, alongside the CERT-In Directions
15 August 2023, on the day both Acts received assent
explanation: The BSA and BNSS came into force on 1 July 2024, replacing the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The CERT-In Directions date from 2022.

q: Which BSA provision is the successor to the Section 65B certificate of the old Evidence Act?
options: Section 57, on primary evidence and proper custody
Section 61, on the admissibility of electronic records
Section 79A, on Examiners of Electronic Evidence
Section 63, with the certificate in the BSA Schedule
explanation: Section 63 deals with the admissibility of electronic records produced as evidence and is accompanied by the Schedule certificate. Section 79A belongs to the IT Act, not the BSA.

q: The BSA Schedule certificate has two parts. Who completes each part?
options: Part A by the party producing the record; Part B by an expert
Part A by the investigating officer; Part B by the magistrate
Part A by the forensic lab; Part B by the opposing counsel
Part A by CERT-In; Part B by the device's manufacturer
explanation: Part A is completed by the party producing the electronic record, typically the person responsible for the device; Part B is completed by an expert.

q: Which technical detail does the BSA Schedule certificate ask for that directly depends on the lab's acquisition record?
options: The examiner's academic qualifications and years of experience
The make of write blocker used to connect the original device
The hash value of the electronic record and the algorithm used
The full list of files found in the device's unallocated space
explanation: The certificate asks for the hash value and algorithm. That value must be the one recorded at acquisition and traceable through custody to the item.

q: The certificate for image KF-031-E01-D1 cites a SHA-256 value. What makes that value meaningful rather than a formality?
options: It was computed with the newest available hashing tool on the day of the hearing
It traces, through the acquisition notes and custody log, to the item and moment it describes
It was computed by the expert who signs Part B, independently of the lab's own acquisition records
It matches the hash of the original laptop's operating-system installation media
explanation: A hash proves identity only between the objects and moments it compares. Its value as evidence comes from the documented chain linking it to the acquisition and the item.

q: Under the explanations to BSA Section 57, when is an electronic record produced from proper custody treated as primary evidence?
options: Only when an Examiner of Electronic Evidence has certified it in writing
Only when it was seized by police with audio-video recording of the seizure
Whenever it is printed and signed by the person who created the record
Unless it is disputed
explanation: The explanation treats an electronic or digital record produced from proper custody as primary evidence unless it is disputed. Custody records help show proper custody.

q: What does BNSS Section 105 require when police conduct a search or take possession of property?
options: Audio-video electronic recording of the process, including preparing the seizure list
A forensic image of every seized device within twenty-four hours of the seizure
Written consent from the owner of each seized device before it is removed
A certificate under BSA Section 63 prepared for every seized item at the time of the seizure itself
explanation: Section 105 requires the search or seizure, including the list of seized items and its signing by witnesses, to be recorded by audio-video means, preferably a mobile phone, and forwarded to the magistrate.

q: Under BNSS Section 176(3), when must a forensic expert visit the crime scene?
options: In every case involving a computer, phone or other electronic device
Only when the accused requests an independent forensic examination
For offences punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more
Only for offences under the Information Technology Act, 2000
explanation: Section 176(3) applies to offences punishable with seven years or more, with the process videographed. States have time to build the necessary facilities, so practice may vary.

q: What does Section 79A of the IT Act provide for?
options: Mandatory six-hour reporting of cyber incidents to CERT-In
Notification by the Central Government of Examiners of Electronic Evidence
Penalties for unauthorised access to a computer system or network
The form of the certificate that must accompany electronic records produced as evidence in court
explanation: Section 79A lets the Central Government notify bodies or departments as Examiners of Electronic Evidence. Incident reporting comes from CERT-In Directions, and the certificate from the BSA.

q: Which set of requirements comes from the CERT-In Directions of 28 April 2022?
options: Report specified incidents within 6 hours, keep logs for 180 days in India, and sync clocks to NIC or NPL NTP
Report incidents within 72 hours, keep logs for one year anywhere, and sync clocks to any public NTP server
Report incidents within 24 hours, keep backups for 90 days, and encrypt all logs with approved algorithms
Report incidents to the police first, keep logs until each case closes, and record clocks only during incidents
explanation: The Directions require six-hour reporting of specified incidents, a rolling 180 days of logs kept within Indian jurisdiction, and clock synchronisation with NIC or NPL NTP servers or servers traceable to them.

q: Why does the lesson treat clock synchronisation under the CERT-In Directions as a forensic matter?
options: Because unsynchronised clocks make electronic records inadmissible in Indian courts
Because CERT-In examiners refuse to review logs from unsynchronised systems
Because synchronised clocks make timelines from different systems comparable without guesswork
Because the BSA certificate requires the clock offset of every system in the organisation to be stated
explanation: Synchronised clocks let examiners align events across systems. The lesson does not claim that unsynchronised clocks make evidence inadmissible; that would be a legal conclusion.

q: Kestrel's investigation was internal for two weeks before a police complaint was filed. What is the main lesson for its records?
options: Internal records are irrelevant once the police begin their own investigation
Internal records should be rewritten in police format before the hand-over
Internal records can be completed from memory once the complaint is filed
Internal evidence should be handled from the start as if it may reach a court
explanation: Internal matters often become legal ones, and contemporaneous records cannot be created afterwards. Rewriting records would undermine them.

q: In the Kestrel hand-over, why does the lab not complete the Section 63 certificate itself?
options: Because only the police may complete certificates for internal evidence
Because the certificate is signed by the responsible person and the expert, so the lab supplies the facts
Because certificates are needed only for evidence seized under BNSS Section 105
Because a lab that has examined the device is disqualified from contributing to any part of the certificate
explanation: The people who sign Parts A and B vouch for its contents. The lab's role is to supply accurate, documented facts so that they can do so truthfully.

q: The firewall export E-04 reached the lab without a manifest. How should the hand-over note treat it?
options: Record that its integrity anchor is the lab's intake hash, not a hash taken at source
Omit E-04 from the hand-over, since items without manifests cannot be produced
Ask IT operations to generate a manifest now and backdate it to the export
Describe E-04 as verified at source in the note, because the lab hashed it immediately on arrival
explanation: The limitation is stated honestly so that nobody assumes source verification. Backdating would be fabrication, and omission hides relevant evidence.

q: In two Supreme Court cases on the old Section 65B, Anvar P.V. (2014) and Arjun Panditrao (2020), what did the Court hold about the certificate?
options: That a certificate was optional when the original device was unavailable
That certificates were required only for evidence from government computers
That the certificate was a condition for admitting secondary electronic evidence
That hash values were mandatory in every certificate under Section 65B
explanation: Both judgments treated the 65B(4) certificate as a condition for admitting secondary electronic evidence. How the BSA provisions are applied now is a question for counsel.

q: An old Kestrel procedure tells staff to 'attach a 65B certificate'. What does the lesson recommend?
options: Keep the procedure unchanged, because courts still use the old section numbers
Delete the step, because certificates are no longer needed under the BSA
Replace it with a reference to BNSS Section 105, which now covers certificates for all seized electronic records
Update it to refer to the current provision, record the change and have counsel confirm the wording
explanation: Out-of-date templates may omit fields such as the hash algorithm. The update is recorded and checked by the legal adviser, since it concerns legal wording.

q: Which statement about the DPDP Act and forensic work matches the lesson?
options: The Act does not apply to any data processed during an internal investigation
The Act has exemptions for investigation, but their application is a legal question, and minimisation is good practice regardless
The Act requires every person whose data appears in an image to give consent before any examination begins, without exception
The Act requires all forensic images to be deleted within 30 days of acquisition
explanation: Exemptions exist, including for prevention, detection, investigation or prosecution of offences, but their scope for a given organisation is for counsel. Minimisation protects people and the investigation either way.

q: Which practice best applies data minimisation to the Kestrel laptop image?
options: Examine only what the authorised scope requires and keep unrelated personal data out of the report
Delete every personal file from the working copy before analysis begins
Share the full image with every interested department so nothing is missed
Copy all personal messages into an appendix of the report so that the court can see the full context
explanation: Minimisation limits examination, access and reporting to the scope. Deleting files from a working copy alters evidence, and broad sharing or copying expands exposure.

q: Under the BNSS, a court or police officer may require a person to produce a document or other thing, expressly including digital evidence. How should an organisation respond to such a requirement?
options: Send the original device immediately to avoid any appearance of delay
Ignore it until a Section 63 certificate has been issued by the police
Route it through the legal adviser and produce a verified, documented copy
Ask the lab to decide which records are relevant and send those only
explanation: Production requests are legal processes. The legal adviser manages the response, and the lab provides a verified copy with its records.

q: Why does the lesson say a strong acquisition with a weak record is legally weaker than a modest acquisition with a complete record?
options: Because courts check evidence through records such as certificates, custody logs and notes
Because modest acquisitions are faster to complete and so leave much less room for human error
Because Indian courts prefer logical copies to full physical images
Because complete records automatically make the evidence admissible
explanation: Legal instruments test evidence indirectly through its records. Complete records do not guarantee admissibility, which is for the court, but they remove grounds for challenge.

q: Which of these decisions belongs to counsel and the court rather than to the forensic lab?
options: Which hash algorithm to record at acquisition
Whether a particular electronic record is admissible
How to word a fact so that it is separate from an opinion
Which custody log entries need a dated correction memorandum
explanation: Admissibility is a legal decision. The lab controls the quality of its records, methods and wording.

q: A Kestrel custody log is kept on a shared drive that any employee can edit. Why is this a legal as well as a security concern?
options: Because shared drives are prohibited for evidence records under the IT Act
Because the CERT-In Directions require custody logs to be held by CERT-In
Because the BSA requires all custody logs to be printed and signed in ink by each custodian
Because anyone could have altered it, which invites a challenge to the record itself
explanation: Evidence records are evidence too. Uncontrolled edit access lets the other side question whether the record was altered. Access controls and hashes on the record defend against this.

q: In Figure 1, which record links the 'Acquisition, examination' row to the 'Production in court' row?
options: The video recording of the seizure made under BNSS Section 105
The organisation's CERT-In incident report submitted within six hours
The hash value and algorithm recorded at acquisition and cited on the certificate
The list of unrelated personal data kept in the minimisation record
explanation: The hash recorded during acquisition reappears in Parts A and B of the certificate, which is why it must be recorded with its algorithm and traced through custody.

q: A matter began before 1 July 2024 and is heard after it. Which law governs the electronic evidence?
options: Always the BSA, because new procedural law applies to every pending case
Always the old Evidence Act, because the conduct occurred before the change
Whichever law the forensic lab's procedure manual refers to
A question for counsel and the court; the lab keeps records that satisfy either
explanation: Transitional questions are legal questions. The lab's job is unchanged: records that let either certificate be completed truthfully.

q: What does BSA Section 61 say about electronic records?
options: That electronic records may be produced in court only with an accompanying certificate issued by CERT-In
That admissibility shall not be denied on the sole ground that a record is electronic or digital
That electronic records are secondary evidence unless printed and signed
That electronic records older than 180 days are presumed to be unreliable
explanation: Section 61 states that the admissibility of a record shall not be denied merely because it is electronic or digital. Other rules, including Section 63, still govern how it is proved.
